candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the hash/signature string passed to approveScript / approveSignature / aclApproveSignature / approveClasspathEntry (request parameters) and controls the content of a sandboxed script they submit for approval. A hash is computable offline (SHA-512 of language name + ':' + script, per Hasher.hash), and a signature is just a StaticWhitelist line such as a static method or field reference the attacker needs at runtime. The attacker does not need Jenkins credentials; they only need an administrator's browser to issue the request.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the mutation methods do enforce Jenkins.ADMINISTER (lines 965, 983, 1001, 1013, 1029, 1099, 1108, 1117, 1125, 1135, 1186, 1213, 1225, 1235), so the issue is not a missing permission check on these methods; checked that SecureGroovyScript.doCheckScript and DescriptorImpl do use @RequirePOST (SecureGroovyScript.java lines 532-533), showing the codebase knows the pattern but does not apply it here; checked setApprovedSignatures/setApprovedScriptHashes validate input (lines 857-874, 897-924) while approveScript/approveSignature do not, so validation cannot compensate; confirmed no @RequirePOST import in ScriptApproval.java. Framework behavior (whether Stapler's @JavaScriptMethod proxy enforces POST or the CSRF crumb filter covers the resulting request) is external to this snapshot and could not be verified, which is the main reason for low confidence.
candidates.impact: Bypass of the human review step that is the core security control of the Script Security plugin: an attacker-chosen script or sandbox signature can be approved without an administrator intentionally deciding to approve it, ultimately permitting sandbox escape/arbitrary code execution on the Jenkins controller under the identity of the victim administrator's approval.
candidates.prerequisites: A Jenkins administrator with ADMINISTER permission must be induced to visit attacker-controlled content (classic CSRF), or the attacker must otherwise cause the administrator's browser/context to request the endpoint. For approveScript, the attacker must know the hash of a script they previously got into the pending list or a script they can get executed later; for approveSignature, any signature string suffices. Exploitability depends on whether the Stapler/JavaScriptMethod layer (external to this snapshot) fails to enforce POST — the snapshot contains no server-side POST/crumb enforcement of its own.
candidates.root_cause: ScriptApproval exposes multiple @JavaScriptMethod endpoints that mutate the approval database (approvedScriptHashes, approvedSignatures, aclApprovedSignatures, approved/pending classpath entries). Each method performs Jenkins.ADMINISTER but carries no @RequirePOST (or other HTTP-method restriction), unlike SecureGroovyScript.doCheckScript which does use @RequirePOST. approveScript(String hash) additionally stores the caller-supplied hash into approvedScriptHashes without validating its format (contrast setApprovedScriptHashes, which validates SHA-512/SHA-1 patterns), and approveSignature(String signature) stores an arbitrary signature string without parsing/validation.
candidates.title: ScriptApproval approve/deny AJAX endpoints lack @RequirePOST, enabling CSRF-driven approval of attacker-chosen scripts/signatures
candidates.trace: 1) An unprivileged user can define an unapproved sandboxed script (e.g. in a Pipeline or another plugin) and cause it to be added to pendingScripts via ScriptApproval.configuring (lines 590-609) or generate the hash offline with Hasher.hash (lines 213-223). 2) The attacker crafts a request to the exposed approve endpoint, e.g. .../scriptApproval/approveScript?hash=<SHA-512 of their script> or .../approveSignature?signature=method java.lang.System getProperty java.lang.String. 3) approveScript (line 964) / approveSignature (line 1098) / aclApproveSignature (line 1107) check Jenkins.ADMINISTER (satisfied by the victim admin's session) and then directly add the supplied value to approvedScriptHashes / approvedSignatures / aclApprovedSignatures, save(), and reconfigure() the ApprovedWhitelist. 4) The attacker's script now passes ScriptApproval.using/checkAndConvertApprovedScript (lines 294-311, 626-638) or their signature is now permitted by the reconfigured whitelist, so the sandbox approval gate is bypassed. No source-level POST/verb check exists in these methods to prevent step 2 from being cross-site.
candidates.unverified: Whether the @JavaScriptMethod endpoints are actually reachable with a GET/non-crumb request in a running Jenkins+Stapler combination could not be verified from this repository (Stapler is not in the snapshot and no tests/Jelly bindings are present). Also unverified: whether the corresponding upstream security fix was exactly the addition of @RequirePOST, and whether a crumb/token check in another layer already mitigates this. No runtime test was executed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-352 Cross-Site Request Forgery; missing HTTP-method restriction on security-critical administrative state change

coverage_summary: Read/reviewed all 49 model-visible files to varying depth: every main Java class in sandbox/groovy (SandboxInterceptor, GroovyCallSiteSelector, GroovySandbox, ClassLoaderWhitelist, SandboxResolvingClassLoader, RejectASTTransformsCustomizer, SecureGroovyScript), sandbox whitelists (EnumeratingWhitelist, StaticWhitelist, ProxyWhitelist, AclAwareWhitelist, AnnotatedWhitelist, BlanketWhitelist, JenkinsWhitelist, GenericWhitelist, Whitelist, AbstractWhitelist), scripts package (ScriptApproval, ClasspathEntry, ApprovalContext, languages, exceptions, notes/links), pom.xml and the 7 resource files. The searchable tree contains only src/main; no tests are present. The whitelist/blacklist definition resources referenced by GenericWhitelist (generic-whitelist), JenkinsWhitelist (jenkins-whitelist) and StaticWhitelist (blacklist) are NOT in the snapshot, so the actual allowed signature sets could not be inspected — this materially limits judging which specific calls are approved and thus limits sandbox-bypass analysis.
limitations: No test sources, no Jelly views, and no whitelist/blacklist resource files (generic-whitelist, jenkins-whitelist, blacklist) are present, so static whitelist contents and UI/AJAX wiring could not be inspected.
Stapler/JavaScriptMethod and CSRF-crumb semantics are external to the snapshot; GET-reachability of the flagged endpoints and any framework-level POST enforcement could not be confirmed.
Groovy runtime dispatch semantics in the dependency jars (Groovy version from the BOM, groovy-sandbox 1.32) could not be inspected, limiting verification of call-site-selection mismatches.
No code was executed and no scanners were run; findings are source-evidence only and are leads, not confirmed vulnerabilities.
The snapshot version/commit is not identified in-tree (version is 999999-SNAPSHOT; CHANGELOG stops at 1.76), so correlation with a known fixed release is inferred, not verified.

rejected_leads.lead: Sandbox bypass via SandboxInterceptor.onMethodCall fallback branches (Map values called as methods, Script binding closure variables, GroovyInterceptable invokeMethod redirection, ClosureMetaMethod) potentially approving a different method than Groovy executes.
rejected_leads.reason: The recursion into onMethodCall still performs a whitelist check for the concrete method that will be invoked; I could construct no source-level dispatch mismatch that reaches a non-whitelisted JDK method. The static whitelist resources that would be needed to judge whether e.g. Closure.call is statically permitted are absent from the snapshot, so this remains speculative.

rejected_leads.lead: GroovyCallSiteSelector method/constructor resolution (varargs emulation, isInstancePrimitive widening/narrowing, isMoreSpecific) disagreeing with Groovy's actual dispatch, so the interceptor approves one overload while another executes.
rejected_leads.reason: The heuristic closely mirrors documented Groovy ParameterTypes behavior and I found no concrete overload pair or parameter sequence in the snapshot demonstrating a check/execute mismatch; proving it would require executing the Groovy runtime, which is disallowed here.

rejected_leads.lead: ScriptApproval.getClasspathRenderInfo (lines 1169-1181) is an @JavaScriptMethod with no Jenkins permission check, exposing pending/approved classpath paths and hashes.
rejected_leads.reason: Information disclosure of classpath paths/hashes only, requires whatever read permission the Stapler proxy enforces, and the same framework uncertainty as the submitted candidate; weaker impact than the approval mutation endpoints and likely part of the same endpoint-hardening theme rather than a separate strong candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: StaticWhitelist / EnumeratingWhitelist signature matching and cache (canonical signatures, wildcard handling, precache/clearCache) could permit unintended methods.
rejected_leads.reason: No specific signature normalization flaw was demonstrated; signature canonicalization uses exact declaring-class and parameter-type names, and the resource files defining the actual approved signatures are missing from the snapshot, preventing any concrete over-permission finding.

rejected_leads.lead: RejectASTTransformsCustomizer blocks only a fixed list of Groovy AST-transform annotations (plus an optional system property list), potentially allowing other compile-time transforms present on the classpath.
rejected_leads.reason: Exploiting this requires a globally registered transform supplied by some other plugin/jar; within this snapshot only the enumerated annotations are reachable and they are blocked, and no attacker-controlled transform registration is present in the reviewed code.

summary: Reviewed the 49-file script-security snapshot (main Java + a few resources; no tests, and notably the whitelist/blacklist resources are absent). The strongest source-supported lead is the complete absence of HTTP-method/CSRF protection on ScriptApproval's state-changing administrative AJAX endpoints, which are the sole gate between "script/signature pending" and "approved" (the approval mechanism the whole plugin depends on). Candidate submitted with low confidence because the framework-level GET-reachability of @JavaScriptMethod endpoints cannot be verified inside this snapshot.
